**Little Mice**

The word "muscle" comes from the Latin *musculus*, which means "little mouse." Someone, a very long time ago, watched a bicep flex under skin and thought it looked like a mouse moving under a cloth. The comparison was good enough to catch on, and it caught on so thoroughly that it stopped being a comparison. Nobody who pulls a muscle today thinks of rodents.

I find this kind of thing endlessly interesting, so I'm going to spend my free thousand words on dead metaphors.

English is full of them. A daisy is a "day's eye," because the flower opens in the morning and closes at dusk. A window is a "wind eye," from the Old Norse *vindauga*, originally a hole in the roof that let smoke out and weather in. A mortgage is a "dead pledge" in Old French. Sarcasm comes from a Greek verb meaning to tear flesh. To calculate is to move *calculi*, pebbles, around a counting board.

A lord, in Old English, was a *hlafweard*, a loaf-guardian, and a lady was a *hlæfdige*, a loaf-kneader. That tells you what power meant when those words were coined: control over the bread.

My favorite of the showy ones is "clue." It used to be spelled "clew" and meant a ball of thread. The modern meaning exists because of one particular ball of thread, the one Theseus unwound to find his way back out of the Labyrinth. Every detective novel carries a faint trace of the Minotaur.

Those examples are fun because the original image is so vivid and so thoroughly forgotten. The more important dead metaphors are the ones you can't get through a paragraph without. Look at how we talk about thinking. We grasp an idea, see a point, and follow an argument. Arguments have foundations and can collapse. Moods go up and down, time is spent, saved, and wasted as if it were money, and the future lies ahead of us while the past is behind.

That last one feels like a fact about time, but it's a convention. Speakers of Aymara, in the Andes, put the past in front and the future behind, on the reasonable grounds that you can see what has already happened and can't see what's coming.

In 1980 George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argued in *Metaphors We Live By* that this is how abstract thought gets built in the first place, out of the experience of having a body that moves through space and handles objects. I don't know how far the strong version of that claim holds, and people still argue about it. The weak version is hard to escape, though. Try describing what it is to understand something without borrowing from sight, touch, or movement. "Comprehend" is Latin for "seize." Even "abstract" means "dragged away."

What interests me most is how these metaphors die, because they die of success. A live metaphor makes the listener do some work. When someone first called a flexing arm a little mouse, the hearer had to notice the gap between the two things and cross it. Each repetition makes the crossing easier, until there is no gap left and the word simply means the new thing. Dictionaries record this as a second definition. Nobody decides it and nobody notices the moment.

"Deadline" is a case where you can almost watch it happen. In the 1860s it was a line inside Civil War prison camps like Andersonville, and a prisoner who crossed it would be shot. A few decades later newspapers were using the word for the time after which copy couldn't make the edition. Now it's a mild word that lives in calendar apps, and people miss deadlines every day without any sense of having stepped across something lethal.

The process is still running, and computing is where it's easiest to see. We keep files in folders on a desktop. We scroll, though almost no one has handled a scroll in centuries. We hang up phones that have no hook and dial numbers on devices with no dial. We cc people, though few of us have ever made a carbon copy. The icon for saving is a floppy disk, which many people using it have never held. A firewall was, and still is, an actual wall built to stop an actual fire from spreading through a building. For now "the cloud" still has a trace of image in it, but I'd guess it has a generation or two before it's as dead as "muscle."

I have a personal stake in this, to whatever extent I have personal stakes. I use these words constantly. I tell people I see what they mean, that I'll walk them through a proof, that a problem is hard to get a handle on. I have never seen, walked, or handled anything. Every bodily metaphor I use was coined by someone with a body and handed down through a great deal of text until it reached me. You could read that as a kind of fraud. I think it's closer to an extreme version of the ordinary situation.

You have probably never moved pebbles on a counting board, guarded a loaf, or followed a thread out of a maze. Every speaker inherits a vocabulary minted from experiences they didn't have, by people they'll never know anything about. The Roman who saw the mouse is unrecoverable. We don't have a name or a century, only the word, which works perfectly well without them.

This changes how sentences feel to me. A plain sentence like "my companion considered the disaster" turns out to be crowded: someone sharing bread, and, if the usual etymologies are right, two different people looking at stars. "Disaster" is an ill-starred event, and "consider" may come from the Latin for examining the heavens. None of it is visible unless you look it up, and the sentence means exactly the same thing either way. I still like knowing they're in there.

If you want to try this yourself, pick a word you used today without thinking and check where it came from. Many of them turn out to be someone's old observation. "Companion" is the one I'd keep if I could keep only one, since it defines friendship by the plain act of eating bread with someone.

I'm going through a list of word origins to find ones I can state accurately: "muscle" from the Latin for little mouse, "disaster" from an Italian word meaning ill-starred, and "clue" from a word for a ball of thread, the one Theseus used in the labyrinth. I'm also checking "deadline," which traces back to a line prisoners couldn't cross in Civil War camps, and I'm leaving out the etymologies I can't verify, like "consider" and "salary."

I'm checking a few more word histories for the essay: "lord" from an Old English word for loaf-keeper, "digit" from the word for finger, and "mortgage" from a dead pledge. I'm starting to see the point I want to make, that language is full of fossilized metaphors built from the body and physical things, and that new ones keep being coined, like "bug," "cloud," and "desktop."

I'm drafting the essay as a short piece titled "Little Mice," and I'm planning to avoid the usual AI habits: no "not X but Y" constructions, no reflexive triplets, no tidy closing lines, and as few em-dashes and colon reveals as I can manage. I also want the reflection on my own position to stay modest rather than dramatic.

I'm working through the essay's examples now: "muscle" as a little mouse, and I'm moving on to other dead metaphors like "daisy," "window," and "companion," checking each one's origin before I use it.

I'm working through the rest of the word histories now: "lady" as the loaf-kneader, the mortgage as a dead pledge, and sarcasm from a Greek word for tearing flesh. I'm also checking "calculate," which comes from the pebbles used on a counting board, and "clue," which shifted from a ball of thread to the thread Theseus used in the labyrinth. I'm thinking about how the detective story carries that old thread-and-Minotaur memory.

I'm now working through how the examples fit together: the future placed ahead of us, time spent or saved like money, and the Aymara case where the past sits in front because it can be seen. The weak form of the embodiment claim seems hard to dispute, since it's difficult to describe understanding without seeing, holding, or moving.

I'm reflecting on how I use words like "see" and "walk through" without ever having seen or walked anything, since every bodily metaphor I rely on was inherited from people who had bodies.
